summary: A white paper discussing accounting requirements for IPng. It recommends that all IPng packets carry accounting tags, which would vary in size. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A note suggesting every packet should have a label for who to bill.

questions: how to bill for network traffic
subtitle: Embedding cost tracking in every packet to simplify billing and resource management.

tldr.problem: Tracking who pays for what in a global network is complex without built-in support.
tldr.mechanism: Add an optional accounting tag to every IPng packet. The tag starts as a simple voucher identifying the responsible party, and can optionally carry higher-layer accounting data (costs, charges).
tldr.outcome: Routers and meters can identify the payer without complex rule tables, and applications can inform users of charges incurred.

today: RFC 1672 is Informational. IPv6 eventually adopted a different approach: a Flow Label field for identifying flows, but no built-in accounting field. Usage-based accounting today relies on NetFlow, IPFIX and other external monitoring tools rather than in-packet tags.

sections.title: Accounting Tags in Packets
sections.content:
RFC 1672 proposes that all IPng packets carry accounting tags—optional fields that identify who pays for each packet. Nevil Brownlee from the University of Auckland builds on a suggestion by Brian Carpenter to include authenticated (source, destination, transaction) triplets in IPng packets.

The RFC recommends two types of tags: a simple voucher for transport-layer accounting, and optionally a separate tag for application-layer variables. This dual approach keeps router and meter administration separate.
sections.plainLanguage: Packets get a label showing who sent it, where it goes, and which user account to charge for it.

sections.title: How Tags Enable Billing
sections.content:
At the transport layer, the tag is simply a voucher—an arbitrary string identifying the party responsible for the packet. The originating host sets it, and it identifies the user who sent the data. Along the packet's path, the tag may be changed as policy-based routing reassigns responsibility. For example, from user to carrier to another carrier as the packet crosses network boundaries.

Accounting meters read the tags to identify traffic flows without needing complex tables of rules. This greatly simplifies accounting for transit traffic across intermediate networks. Applications can also use a separate application-level tag to inform users of costs.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet says 'this user sent it' or 'this company is paying for it', so billing happens automatically as routers and meters count packets.

sections.title: Tag Structure
sections.content:
The RFC proposes keeping the transport voucher as part of the routing tuple. A separate application-level tag could carry higher-layer variables (charges, resource usage) in a standardized list format. If encryption overhead becomes too high, the two tags could be combined.

The RFC does not specify the exact format or variable packing; it leaves those details to future work by the Accounting Working Group. For IPng, the key requirement is simply that the protocol can carry one or two variable-size objects in every packet.
sections.plainLanguage: Packets need space for a short billing label and optionally a longer cost record, but the exact format can be decided later.

sections.title: Secure Accounting
sections.content:
For accounting to work in a hostile environment, the tags must be tamper-proof. Routers and meters need cryptographic keys to verify them. Network operators must plan key distribution—deciding which routers need which keys—much as they do for policy-based routing. This overhead is acceptable because it is necessary anyway for reliable policy-based routing.

The RFC notes that tags carrying authentication information must remain unforgeable so that charges reflect actual usage, not false claims.
sections.plainLanguage: Billing labels need to be signed so nobody can fake charges. Routers need passwords to check the signatures.
